prompt: In aromatic nitration, how many times more reactive than benzene does an –OH substituent make the ring?
explanation: Substituents affect the reactivity of the ring. In aromatic nitration, an –OH substituent makes the ring 1000 times more reactive than benzene, while an –NO2 substituent makes it more than 10 million times less reactive.

prompt: In aromatic nitration, how does an –NO2 substituent affect the reactivity of the ring compared with benzene?

choices.text: It makes the ring more than 10 million times less reactive
It makes the ring about 1000 times less reactive
choices.why: 1000 is the factor for –OH, which makes the ring 1000 times more reactive. –NO2 slows the reaction by more than 10 million times.

choices.text: It makes the ring more than 10 million times more reactive
choices.why: –NO2 is a deactivating group: it withdraws electrons and makes the ring less reactive.

choices.text: It has almost no effect, because it doesn't bond to the ring through a lone pair
choices.why: –NO2 has a huge effect: it makes the ring more than 10 million times less reactive.

explanation: In aromatic nitration, an –OH substituent makes the ring 1000 times more reactive than benzene, while an –NO2 substituent makes the ring more than 10 million times less reactive. Nitro is a strongly deactivating, meta-directing group.

prompt: Which class of substituent does NOT exist in electrophilic aromatic substitution?

choices.text: Meta-directing activators
Ortho- and para-directing deactivators
choices.why: These exist: the halogens are deactivating but ortho- and para-directing.

choices.text: Meta-directing deactivators
choices.why: These exist: –NO2, –CN, –CHO, –CO2H, and other groups are meta-directing deactivators.

choices.text: Ortho- and para-directing activators
choices.why: These exist: –CH3, –OH, and –NHCOCH3 are ortho- and para-directing activators.

explanation: Substituents fall into three groups (Figure 16.4.1): ortho- and para-directing activators, ortho- and para-directing deactivators, and meta-directing deactivators. There are no meta-directing activators. All meta-directing groups are strongly deactivating.

prompt: What makes halogen substituents unique among the groups in Figure 16.4.1?

choices.text: They are deactivating but ortho- and para-directing
They are activating but meta-directing
choices.why: There are no meta-directing activators. Halogens are weakly deactivating and ortho- and para-directing.

choices.text: They are strongly activating and ortho- and para-directing
choices.why: Many groups, such as –OH, are activating ortho/para directors. Halogens are unusual because they deactivate the ring.

choices.text: They are strongly deactivating and meta-directing
choices.why: That describes groups such as –NO2 and –CHO. Halogens are only weakly deactivating, and they direct ortho and para.

explanation: All activating groups are ortho- and para-directing, and all deactivating groups other than halogen are meta-directing. Halogens are unique in being deactivating but ortho- and para-directing (Figure 16.4.1).

prompt: According to the section's table of nitration results, what percentage of the product from nitration of toluene is the ortho isomer?
explanation: Nitration of toluene gives 63% ortho, 3% meta, and 34% para product. The methyl group is an ortho- and para-directing activator.

prompt: According to the section's table of nitration results, what percentage of the product from nitration of chlorobenzene is the para isomer?
explanation: Nitration of chlorobenzene gives 35% ortho, 1% meta, and 64% para product. Chlorine is deactivating but ortho- and para-directing.

prompt: According to the section's table of nitration results, what percentage of the product from nitration of benzaldehyde (C6H5CHO) is the meta isomer?
explanation: Nitration of benzaldehyde gives 19% ortho, 72% meta, and 9% para product. The –CHO group is a meta-directing deactivator.

prompt: According to the section's table of nitration results, what percentage of the product from nitration of nitrobenzene is the meta isomer?
explanation: Nitration of nitrobenzene gives 7% ortho, 91% meta, and 2% para product, so m-dinitrobenzene dominates. –NO2 is a strongly deactivating meta director.

prompt: Nitration of chlorobenzene gives 35% ortho, 1% meta, and 64% para product. What total percentage is substituted ortho or para to the chlorine?
explanation: 35% + 64% = 99%. Even though chlorine deactivates the ring, nearly all substitution occurs ortho or para to it, because its lone pairs stabilize the ortho and para intermediates by resonance.

prompt: According to the section's table of nitration results, which isomer is the major product of the nitration of acetanilide, C6H5NHCOCH3?

choices.text: The para isomer, 79%
The ortho isomer, 79%
choices.why: The –NHCOCH3 row gives 19% ortho and 79% para; para is the major product.

choices.text: The meta isomer, 72%
choices.why: –NHCOCH3 is an ortho- and para-directing activator; only 2% meta product forms. 72% meta is the figure for –CHO.

choices.text: Equal amounts of ortho and para, 50% each
choices.why: That 50:50 split is the result for phenol (–OH). Acetanilide gives 19% ortho and 79% para.

explanation: The nitration table lists –NHCOCH3 as an ortho- and para-directing activator, giving 19% ortho, 2% meta, and 79% para product. So p-nitroacetanilide is the major product.

prompt: Which substituent is a meta-directing deactivator?

choices.text: –CN
–CH3
choices.why: An alkyl group is an ortho- and para-directing activator; nitration of toluene gives only 3% meta product.

choices.text: –Br
choices.why: Halogens are deactivating but ortho- and para-directing; bromobenzene gives only 1% meta product on nitration.

choices.text: –NHCOCH3
choices.why: –NHCOCH3 is an ortho- and para-directing activator; it gives only 2% meta product on nitration.

explanation: The meta-directing deactivators in the section include –N+(CH3)3, –NO2, –CO2H, –CN, –CO2CH3, –COCH3, and –CHO. Nitration of benzonitrile (C6H5CN) gives 81% meta product.

prompt: What is the major product of the sulfonation of toluene with SO3 and H2SO4?

choices.text: A mixture of o-toluenesulfonic acid and p-toluenesulfonic acid
Mainly m-toluenesulfonic acid
choices.why: An alkyl substituent is ortho- and para-directing, so very little meta product forms.

choices.text: Benzenesulfonic acid, by replacement of the methyl group
choices.why: Electrophilic substitution replaces a ring hydrogen; the methyl group stays.

choices.text: Equal amounts of the ortho, meta, and para acids
choices.why: The methyl group directs substitution ortho and para; the three isomers don't form equally.

explanation: Worked Example 16.4.1: according to Figure 16.4.1, an alkyl substituent is ortho- and para-directing, so sulfonation of toluene primarily gives a mixture of o-toluenesulfonic acid and p-toluenesulfonic acid.

prompt: Which ranks these compounds from most to least reactive toward electrophilic substitution: nitrobenzene, phenol, toluene, benzene?

choices.text: Phenol > toluene > benzene > nitrobenzene
Toluene > phenol > benzene > nitrobenzene
choices.why: Both groups activate, but –OH is the stronger activator; Exercise 16.4.1 puts phenol first.

choices.text: Phenol > benzene > toluene > nitrobenzene
choices.why: An alkyl group is activating, so toluene is more reactive than benzene.

choices.text: Nitrobenzene > benzene > toluene > phenol
choices.why: This is reversed. –NO2 strongly deactivates the ring, and –OH strongly activates it.

explanation: Exercise 16.4.1a: phenol > toluene > benzene > nitrobenzene. –OH is a strong activator (1000 times faster than benzene in nitration), –CH3 is a weaker activator, and –NO2 is a strong deactivator (more than 10 million times slower).

prompt: Which ranks these compounds from most to least reactive toward electrophilic substitution: benzene, bromobenzene, benzaldehyde, aniline?

choices.text: Aniline > benzene > bromobenzene > benzaldehyde
Aniline > bromobenzene > benzene > benzaldehyde
choices.why: Halogens are deactivating, so bromobenzene is less reactive than benzene.

choices.text: Benzene > aniline > bromobenzene > benzaldehyde
choices.why: –NH2 is an activating group, so aniline is more reactive than benzene.

choices.text: Aniline > benzene > benzaldehyde > bromobenzene
choices.why: Halogens are only weakly deactivating, while –CHO is strongly deactivating, so benzaldehyde is the least reactive.

explanation: Exercise 16.4.1c: aniline > benzene > bromobenzene > benzaldehyde. –NH2 is activating, –Br is weakly deactivating, and –CHO, like all meta directors, is strongly deactivating.

prompt: What are the major products of the nitration of bromobenzene?

choices.text: o- and p-Bromonitrobenzene
m-Bromonitrobenzene
choices.why: Halogens are ortho- and para-directing; bromobenzene gives only 1% meta product on nitration.

choices.text: No product, because bromine deactivates the ring too strongly
choices.why: Halogens are only weakly deactivating. Bromobenzene is nitrated, mainly ortho and para.

choices.text: Nitrobenzene, by replacement of the bromine
choices.why: Electrophilic substitution replaces a ring hydrogen, so the bromine stays on the ring.

explanation: Exercise 16.4.2a: bromine is an ortho- and para-directing deactivator, so nitration of bromobenzene gives o- and p-bromonitrobenzene (43% ortho, 1% meta, 56% para in the nitration table).

prompt: What is the major product of the bromination of nitrobenzene?

choices.text: m-Bromonitrobenzene
o- and p-Bromonitrobenzene
choices.why: –NO2 is a meta director; it gives very little ortho or para product.

choices.text: Bromobenzene, by replacement of the nitro group
choices.why: Electrophilic substitution replaces a ring hydrogen; the nitro group stays.

choices.text: p-Bromonitrobenzene only
choices.why: –NO2 directs incoming groups meta to itself; nitration of nitrobenzene, for example, gives only 2% para product.

explanation: Exercise 16.4.2b: the nitro group is a strongly deactivating meta director, so bromination of nitrobenzene gives m-bromonitrobenzene. (By contrast, chlorination of phenol and bromination of aniline give ortho and para products.)

prompt: What do all activating groups have in common?

choices.text: They donate electrons to the ring, stabilizing the carbocation intermediate
They withdraw electrons from the ring, making it more electrophilic
choices.why: Withdrawing electrons is what deactivating groups do; it destabilizes the carbocation intermediate.

choices.text: They all have a lone pair on the atom bonded to the ring
choices.why: Alkyl groups activate the ring without a lone pair, by an inductive (hyperconjugative) effect.

choices.text: They raise the energy of the starting aromatic ring so that its aromaticity is lost
choices.why: Activating groups work by stabilizing the carbocation intermediate through electron donation.

explanation: All activating groups donate electrons to the ring, making it more electron-rich, stabilizing the carbocation intermediate, and lowering the activation energy for its formation. All deactivating groups withdraw electrons, destabilizing the intermediate and raising the activation energy.

prompt: Electrostatic potential maps are compared for benzene, benzaldehyde, chlorobenzene, and phenol. Which compound has the most electron-rich (most negative, red) ring?

choices.text: Phenol
Benzaldehyde
choices.why: –CHO is electron-withdrawing, so benzaldehyde's ring is more positive (yellow-green) than benzene's.

choices.text: Chlorobenzene
choices.why: –Cl withdraws electrons overall, so the ring of chlorobenzene is more positive than benzene's.

choices.text: Benzene
choices.why: Benzene is the reference. An electron-donating group such as –OH makes the ring more negative than benzene's.

explanation: Figure 16.4.2 shows that the ring is more positive (yellow-green) when an electron-withdrawing group such as –CHO or –Cl is present, and more negative (red) when an electron-donating group such as –OH is present. Phenol is activated, benzaldehyde deactivated, and chlorobenzene weakly deactivated.

prompt: What is a resonance effect, as the section defines it?

choices.text: Electron donation or withdrawal through a π bond, by p-orbital overlap with the ring
Withdrawal or donation of electrons through a σ bond because of electronegativity
choices.why: That's an inductive effect, as in Section 2.1.

choices.text: Donation of electrons by an alkyl group through hyperconjugation
choices.why: Hyperconjugation is how alkyl groups donate electrons inductively, not a resonance effect.

choices.text: Withdrawal of electrons through space by a nearby charged atom
choices.why: The section defines a resonance effect as electron flow through a π bond by p-orbital overlap.

explanation: A resonance effect is the withdrawal or donation of electrons through a π bond due to the overlap of a p orbital on the substituent with a p orbital on the aromatic ring. An inductive effect is the withdrawal or donation of electrons through a σ bond due to electronegativity.

prompt: Which substituent withdraws electrons from an aromatic ring by resonance?

choices.text: –NO2
–OCH3
choices.why: An alkoxyl group has lone pairs on oxygen, which it donates to the ring by resonance.

choices.text: –NH2
choices.why: An amino group donates its nitrogen lone pair to the ring by resonance.

choices.text: –Cl
choices.why: Halogens withdraw electrons inductively but donate lone-pair electrons by resonance.

explanation: Carbonyl, cyano, and nitro substituents withdraw electrons from the ring by resonance: π electrons flow from the ring to the substituent. Such groups have the general structure –Y=Z, where Z is more electronegative than Y. Halogen, hydroxyl, alkoxyl, and amino groups donate electrons by resonance.

prompt: Hydroxyl, alkoxyl, and amino groups withdraw electrons inductively. Why are they still activators?

choices.text: Their strong resonance donation outweighs their weaker inductive withdrawal
Their inductive effect is electron-donating, like an alkyl group's
choices.why: Their inductive effect is withdrawing, because O and N are electronegative. The resonance effect wins.

choices.text: They have no resonance effect, so only a weak inductive effect is left
choices.why: They have a strong electron-donating resonance effect from the lone pair on O or N.

choices.text: Their stronger electron-withdrawing resonance effect makes the ring a better electrophile
choices.why: The ring reacts as a nucleophile; withdrawing electrons would deactivate it. These groups donate by resonance.

explanation: When the two effects act in opposite directions, the stronger effect dominates. Hydroxyl, alkoxyl, and amino substituents are activators because their stronger electron-donating resonance effect outweighs their weaker electron-withdrawing inductive effect.

prompt: Why are halogen substituents deactivators?

choices.text: Their strong inductive withdrawal outweighs their weaker resonance donation
They withdraw electrons both inductively and by resonance
choices.why: Halogens donate electrons by resonance through their lone pairs; that donation is just weaker than their inductive withdrawal.

choices.text: Their resonance donation outweighs their inductive withdrawal
choices.why: That's the case for –OH, –OR, and –NH2, which are activators. For halogens the inductive withdrawal is stronger.

choices.text: They have a positively polarized atom directly attached to the ring
choices.why: That describes meta directors such as –CHO. Halogens are electronegative and carry lone pairs.

explanation: Halogens are deactivators because their stronger electron-withdrawing inductive effect outweighs their weaker electron-donating resonance effect (Table 16.4.1: strong withdrawing inductive, weak donating resonance).

prompt: Using the classification of substituent effects, why do Friedel–Crafts alkylations often give polysubstitution while acylations do not?

choices.text: Alkylbenzenes are more reactive than benzene, but acylbenzenes are less reactive
Alkylbenzenes are less reactive than benzene, but acylbenzenes are more reactive
choices.why: This is reversed. Alkyl groups activate the ring; acyl (carbonyl) groups deactivate it.

choices.text: Both products are more reactive than benzene, but acyl groups are too large to add twice
choices.why: The acylbenzene is less reactive than benzene, because a carbonyl group is a deactivating meta director.

choices.text: Acyl cations rearrange, while alkyl carbocations don't
choices.why: Acyl cations don't rearrange, and the question is about reactivity of the products, not rearrangement.

explanation: Exercise 16.4.3: an alkyl group is an ortho- and para-directing activator, so the monoalkylated product reacts faster than benzene and is alkylated again. An acyl group is a deactivating meta director, so the acylbenzene reacts more slowly than benzene and acylation stops after one substitution.

prompt: Would (trifluoromethyl)benzene, C6H5CF3, be more or less reactive than toluene toward electrophilic substitution?

choices.text: Less reactive, because the trifluoromethyl group is electron-withdrawing
More reactive, because CF3 is an alkyl group like CH3
choices.why: Unlike CH3, the CF3 group carries three electronegative fluorines and withdraws electrons from the ring.

choices.text: More reactive, because the fluorine lone pairs donate electrons to the ring by resonance
choices.why: Resonance donation needs a lone pair on the atom bonded to the ring. Here carbon is attached to the ring, and the group withdraws electrons.

choices.text: About the same, because both have one carbon attached to the ring
choices.why: The fluorines make CF3 electron-withdrawing, so the ring is less reactive than toluene's.

explanation: Exercise 16.4.4: toluene is more reactive. The methyl group donates electrons inductively, but the trifluoromethyl group is electron-withdrawing, which makes the ring more electron-poor and less reactive toward electrophiles.

prompt: Why are the ortho and para intermediates in the nitration of toluene more stable than the meta intermediate?

choices.text: Only they have a resonance form with the positive charge on the tertiary, methyl-bearing carbon
They have a resonance form in which a lone pair on the methyl group stabilizes the charge
choices.why: A methyl group has no lone pair. It stabilizes the tertiary positive charge by its electron-donating inductive effect.

choices.text: The meta intermediate is less stable because it has only one resonance form
choices.why: All three intermediates are resonance-stabilized. Only ortho and para have a form with the charge on the tertiary, methyl-bearing carbon.

choices.text: The methyl group withdraws electrons inductively from the meta position, destabilizing it
choices.why: Alkyl groups donate electrons. The key is whether the positive charge can sit on the methyl-bearing carbon.

explanation: For both the ortho and para reactions of toluene, but not for meta, a resonance form places the positive charge directly on the methyl-substituted carbon. There it is in a tertiary position and is stabilized by the methyl group's electron-donating inductive effect, so the ortho and para intermediates form faster (Figure 16.4.3).

prompt: Why are the ortho and para intermediates in the nitration of phenol more stable than the meta intermediate?

choices.text: They have an extra resonance form in which oxygen donates electrons to the positive charge
The oxygen withdraws electrons inductively from the ortho and para positions
choices.why: Inductive withdrawal would destabilize a carbocation. The extra stability comes from resonance donation by oxygen.

choices.text: The positive charge is tertiary in the ortho and para intermediates
choices.why: That's the explanation for alkyl groups. For –OH, the key is an extra resonance form with electron donation from oxygen.

choices.text: The meta intermediate is the only aromatic one, so it forms more slowly than the others
choices.why: None of the carbocation intermediates is aromatic. The ortho and para ones have an extra, especially favorable resonance form.

explanation: The ortho and para intermediates from phenol have more resonance forms, including a particularly favorable one in which the positive charge is stabilized by electron donation from the substituent oxygen atom. The meta intermediate has no such stabilization (Figure 16.4.4); nitration of phenol gives 50% ortho, 0% meta, and 50% para.

prompt: Halogens deactivate the ring. Why do they still direct substitution ortho and para?

choices.text: Weak lone-pair resonance donation stabilizes only the ortho and para intermediates
Their inductive withdrawal is felt only at the meta position
choices.why: The section explains the orientation by the halogen's resonance donation, which is felt only at the ortho and para positions.

choices.text: A positively polarized halogen atom makes the meta intermediate unfavorable
choices.why: Halogens are electronegative and carry lone pairs; the δ+ argument applies to meta directors such as –CHO.

choices.text: The halogen is too large to allow substitution at the meta position
choices.why: The reason is electronic: lone-pair donation stabilizes the ortho and para intermediates.

explanation: Although weak, a halogen's electron-donating resonance effect is felt only at the ortho and para positions. A halogen can stabilize the positive charge of the ortho and para intermediates in the same way hydroxyl and amino groups can, while the meta intermediate has no such stabilization and forms more slowly (Figure 16.4.5).

prompt: Why is the meta intermediate favored in the nitration of benzaldehyde?

choices.text: Only ortho and para attack put positive charge on the –CHO-bearing carbon
The meta intermediate has a resonance form in which the carbonyl oxygen donates a lone pair to the ring
choices.why: The carbonyl group withdraws electrons; it doesn't donate to the ring. The meta intermediate is favored because it avoids an unfavorable form.

choices.text: The –CHO group activates the meta position by donating electrons to it
choices.why: –CHO is a deactivator; it withdraws electrons from the ring rather than donating them.

choices.text: The aldehyde group blocks the ortho and para positions by its size
choices.why: The section's reason is electronic: positive charge next to the δ+ carbonyl carbon is disfavored.

explanation: The meta intermediate has three favorable resonance forms, whereas the ortho and para intermediates have only two. In each of those, the third form places the positive charge on the carbon bearing the aldehyde group, next to the positively polarized C=O carbon, a repulsive interaction (Figure 16.4.6).

prompt: According to the section's general rule, how does a substituent that has a positively polarized atom (δ+) directly attached to the ring act?

choices.text: As a meta director
As an ortho and para director
choices.why: A δ+ atom next to the ring makes one resonance form of the ortho and para intermediates unfavorable, so it directs meta.

choices.text: As an activator
choices.why: Such groups withdraw electrons, so they deactivate the ring. There are no meta-directing activators.

choices.text: It has no effect on orientation
choices.why: It strongly affects orientation: nitration of C6H5N+(CH3)3, whose nitrogen bears a positive charge, gives 87% meta product.

explanation: In general, any substituent that has a positively polarized atom directly attached to the ring makes one of the resonance forms of the ortho and para intermediates unfavorable and so acts as a meta director. Examples include –CHO, –NO2, and –N+(CH3)3.

prompt: In the nitration of benzaldehyde, how many favorable resonance forms does the meta carbocation intermediate have?
explanation: The meta intermediate has three favorable resonance forms, while the ortho and para intermediates have only two each. Their third form is unfavorable because it puts the positive charge on the carbon bearing the –CHO group (Figure 16.4.6).
